source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: 800 short Python functions (3-13 lines, no hard arithmetic) test whether LLMs can trace code on a concrete input (output prediction) and work backward (input prediction). Even strong models fail often on programs a CS graduate does in about a minute.
numbers: GPT-4 no CoT: 67% input, 63% output pass@1. GPT-4 with CoT: 74.8% input, 81.9% output. Best open model (Code Llama 34B): about 47% input and 44% output without CoT. Twenty models tested.
limits: Version 1 of the paper (Jan 2024). Programs generated by Code Llama 34B from 69 stdlib functions (str, dict, list only), so scope is narrow.
agent_relevance: Plain code-run tracing is not solved by a frontier model alone; S2 needs a way to check the trace, not trust it.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: Chain of thought helps output prediction (step-by-step execution) more than input prediction, and helps GPT-4 far more than weaker models.
numbers: CoT does not help Code Llama 13B on either task, and does not help GPT-3.5 on input prediction. GPT-4 CoT scored 0/10 on 54 output tasks and 65 input tasks; 22 problems were 0/10 on both.
limits: Gains depend on model strength. CoT widens the gap between pass@1 and pass@5, so samples become more diverse.
agent_relevance: Writing the trace out is only useful if the model is strong enough to follow it. Scaffold value depends on model tier.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution
finding: Training on benchmark-like data does not fix execution tracing. Models distilled on GPT-4 data raised HumanEval but not CRUXEval, so code writing and code tracing are separable skills.
numbers: WizardCoder 34B and Phind 34B scored over 20 points above Code Llama 34B on HumanEval but showed no matching gain on CRUXEval. Phi-1 was strong on HumanEval and among the worst on CRUXEval. Fine-tuning Code Llama 34B on near-benchmark programs reached GPT-4-level but plateaued below 70% on both tasks.
limits: HumanEval scores were taken from reports, not rerun. Base models still show a positive HumanEval-CRUXEval trend.
agent_relevance: A model that writes good code may not hold an accurate model of how the code runs. Do not assume code skill implies trace skill.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: REval tests four runtime-behavior tasks (coverage prediction, program state prediction, execution path prediction, output prediction) and a consistency score that checks whether later answers agree with earlier ones. Most LLMs are weak at both.
numbers: Across the tested LLMs, average accuracy 44.4% on runtime behavior reasoning and average Incremental Consistency score 10.3 (abstract). GPT-4-Turbo average 75.0% and IC 42.5; GPT-3.5-Turbo about 55.7% in the text; best open model CodeLlama-34B-Instruct 51.0%.
limits: Built on HumanEval and ClassEval (Python only). Table text garbled in extraction, so per-task values are not recorded. The 55.7% and 75.0% figures may refer to different averaging.
agent_relevance: A correct final output can hide a wrong path. The agent should check intermediate state, not only the answer.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: CoT prompting improves small-model execution-path prediction. Code-tuned derivatives gain little in runtime reasoning over their base model.
numbers: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct: execution path prediction rose from 10.8% to 21.4% with CoT, beating the 13B model (14.4%). Fine-tuned derivatives improved code reasoning only a little over CodeLlama-7B-Python.
limits: Single prompt template; 7B model case.
agent_relevance: Tracing prompts help weaker models most on path-type questions.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: The founding LLM result: models fail to execute programs in one pass, but writing the intermediate steps (a trace of variable states) into a scratchpad lifts accuracy, in both few-shot and fine-tuned modes.
numbers: Synthetic Python execution (200 test problems): direct 11% few-shot, 20% fine-tuned; scratchpad 26.5% few-shot (relaxed scoring on v0) and 41.5% fine-tuned. Polynomial evaluation: 8.8% to 20.1% few-shot, 31.8% to 50.7% fine-tuned. Addition trained on 1-8 digits: 9-10 digit generalization fails completely without a scratchpad.
limits: 137B decoder model; few-shot scratchpad scoring had to be relaxed because the model would not name the output variable, so 26.5% is not strictly comparable. Best result is still under 50%.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2: a written step-by-step trace beats answering directly. Still far from perfect, so verify with a real run when possible.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: Trace correctness is much harder than output correctness, and incorrect programs still give useful training signal for tracing.
numbers: The paper reports scratchpad beating direct execution on real programs and that exact-match trace accuracy is lower than output accuracy; details of Section 5.2 only partly read.
limits: Only the synthetic-program table was read in full.
agent_relevance: Score traces step by step, not by the last line.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Code Execution with Pre-trained Language Models (CodeExecutor)
finding: A transformer pre-trained on execution traces (mutation-based dataset plus curriculum learning) predicts traces much better than few-shot Codex, but is still weak on hard realistic programs.
numbers: CodeNetMut test split: output accuracy 48.06% and exact trace accuracy 33.38%; the text says a gain of 30.6 points over Codex on output. Tutorial set: 76.42% vs Codex 13.07% output accuracy. Removing curriculum learning dropped output from 48.06% to 45.93% and trace from 33.38% to 30.98%.
limits: Codex could not produce traces in a uniform format on two datasets, so only output accuracy is compared there. Model has a rudimentary grasp of multi-line control flow and is weaker on tuples, dictionaries and sets.
agent_relevance: Trace skill is tied to training distribution; do not expect it to transfer to unusual data structures.

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching Large Language Models to Reason about Code Execution
finding: Showing the model the execution trace (variable states per executed line) helps program repair, but plain CoT over traces is unreliable; self-training on trace-aware rationales gives large gains.
numbers: PaLM 2-L fix rate rose 26.1 points absolute on Mbpp-R and 14.3 on HumanEvalFix-Plus. Removing traces at test time cost an average of 4.8 points (Mbpp-R) and 4.3 (HumanEvalFix-Plus) for CoT. Without traces at test time the NExT model still reached 40.8% (21.8 points above the 3-shot baseline, 3.3 below in-distribution). Only around 30% of base PaLM 2-L rationales explained the bug correctly.
limits: Needs a training loop (not prompt-only). Gains measured on repair, not on tracing itself. Base model hallucinated exceptions not in the trace.
agent_relevance: A real execution trace given to the agent beats a self-imagined one. The imagined-trace route has a hallucination risk.

source: Liu, Chen and Jabbarvand (2026) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for Implicit and Explicit Code Execution Reasoning
finding: Three tasks: independent execution reasoning (IER, trace a given input), specification reasoning (use a test in the spec when writing code), dynamic semantics reasoning. They rank models differently, so one benchmark is not enough.
numbers: 13 LLMs, 4 benchmarks. IER: frontier reasoning models beat the best non-reasoning API model GPT-4 by 14.76 pts (Claude-Sonnet-4.6), 11.35 (o4-mini), 9.26 (DeepSeek-R1); DeepSeek-R1 IER rate 90.43%; DeepSeekCoder-Inst 6.7b 45.54% to 33b 60.23%. Adding one ground-truth test to the spec raised code pass@1 by 5.36% on average (HumanEval 0.94%, ClassEval 9.78%).
limits: Version 6 (April 2026). The spec-test gain is small on clear specs; most of it comes from ambiguous ones.
agent_relevance: A concrete input-output example helps mostly when the task spec is vague. S2 value is highest on ambiguous tasks.

source: Liu, Chen and Jabbarvand (2026) CodeMind: Evaluating LLMs for Implicit and Explicit Code Execution Reasoning
finding: Execution-reasoning skill does not predict bug-repair skill for most models. Repair success mostly comes from pattern matching, not from tracing.
numbers: Abstract: performance in bug repair is not correlated with any of the code reasoning tasks, except for advanced frontier models. Complexity metrics (nesting, recursion, longer loops, non-primitive types) show moderate to strong negative Spearman correlation with reasoning scores. SemCoder-S, fine-tuned on execution data, beat larger DeepSeekCoder-Inst-33b by 3.74 pts and CodeLlama-34B by 9.33 pts on dynamic semantics reasoning.
limits: Correlations are across 13 models only.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a model that can trace to use tracing when debugging. The scaffold must force the trace step.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Assessing Coherency and Consistency of Code Execution Reasoning by LLMs (CES, ICSE 2026)
finding: Right answers can come from wrong traces. Checking each intermediate step shows that many correct outputs are shortcuts, and that reasoning is inconsistent across tests.
numbers: 16 LLMs (3 reasoning). 81.42% of execution simulations on HumanEval were coherent; of those, 46.92% gave correct and 53.08% incorrect output. Consistency across tests: 48.87% random, 45.37% weak. GPT-4 and DeepSeek-R1 had the most incoherent reasoning, mostly from natural-language shortcuts.
limits: Coherence is judged against commonsense execution logic, not exact states.
agent_relevance: Score the trace, not only the final answer. A correct answer after an incoherent trace should not count as success.

source: Haque et al. (2025) Towards Effectively Leveraging Execution Traces for Program Repair with Code LLMs
finding: Adding raw execution traces to repair prompts gives only limited gains: better in just 2 of 6 dataset/model settings. Gains shrink as trace complexity grows. LLM-optimized trace formats help more consistently.
numbers: GPT-3.5 did not benefit (sometimes worse); GPT-4 got a significant lift on two of three datasets.
limits: GPT family only; three repair datasets. The failure to benefit is a boundary condition for trace prompting.
agent_relevance: Long raw traces can hurt. Compress or select trace parts before giving them to the agent.

source: Yeltekin and Bauer (2026) Can LLMs Simulate Novice Programmers' Misconceptions?
finding: Frontier and 30B models solve simple CS1 code-tracing items almost perfectly. Small models do not. LLMs can follow a given misconception, but code-tuned models often slip back to correct execution.
numbers: 13 LLMs, 60 items from 30 ProgMiscon Python misconceptions. Multiple-choice/true-false: 100% for Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 models; Qwen2.5 7B and Qwen2.5-coder 7B 83.3%. Open-ended (27 items): Opus 100%, Qwen2.5 7B 63.0%. Following the misconception: Opus 5 96.7%; Qwen3-coder 30B 45.0% (53.3% answered correctly instead); Qwen2.5 7B 38.3%. Diagnosing the misconception from a wrong answer: 55.0% to 91.7% (free text).
limits: Items written by an LLM with manual review; only 27 of 60 were solvable without answer options; short poster-style paper. Models simulate behaviour; this does not show they hold a notional machine.
agent_relevance: On simple items an LLM is a good tracer. The weak point is complexity and deliberate faulty-model simulation, not basic tracing.

source: Crichton, Agrawala and Hanrahan (2021) The Role of Working Memory in Program Tracing (CHI)
finding: Humans tracing code hold about 7 variable-value pairs in working memory, and swap values between variables under load. Mental arithmetic lowers capacity.
numbers: Cued-recall experiment (15 participants): about 7 pairs, mean around 7.5 with large spread. Tracing: substitution errors 70% more common than calculation errors; error timing differed with arithmetic (chi-square 25.57, p < .001). Strategy experiment (12 of 15 kept): half traced linearly, half on demand from the bottom; 9 of 12 used one strategy 70% of the time or more; on-demand tracers made more WM errors on straight-line code but equal on code with functions.
limits: Small N, online recruitment, restricted-focus interface; mostly straight-line programs.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for why a written trace helps: it replaces a bounded working memory. An agent trace should store state outside the text stream and re-read it.

source: Lister et al. (2004) A multi-national study of reading and tracing skills in novice programmers (ITiCSE working group)
finding: The founding follow-up to McCracken: many novices cannot predict simple code output or complete near-finished code, so weak problem solving is not the only cause of poor results.
numbers: 12 multiple-choice questions, 7 countries. 941 students contributed; 556 answered all 12. Score quartiles: top 10-12 (27%), 8-9 (24%), 5-7 (25%), bottom 0-4 (23%). Excluding the biggest institution (N=228): top 20%, bottom 29%. 37 students interviewed; doodle data from 56 students.
limits: Convenience samples; mixed grading regimes (some took the test for grades, some volunteered); MCQ format.
agent_relevance: Even simple tracing is a fragile skill in humans. Do not assume the agent is better than a weak novice without measuring.

source: Lister et al. (2004) A multi-national study of reading and tracing skills in novice programmers (ITiCSE working group)
finding: Writing the trace down (doodling) goes with the correct answer. Students who wrote nothing got about half right.
numbers: Correct rate by doodle type (N=56): synchronized trace 77% (73 data points); trace 75% (215); odd trace 78% (23); numbers 70% (189); computation 60%; position marks 64%; blank page 50% (256 data points).
limits: Observational, not randomized: better students may doodle more. Blank page also covers easy items and expert shortcuts.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as scratchpads for LLMs: an external trace goes with higher accuracy. Supports a written S2 step.

source: Xie, Nelson and Ko (2018) An Explicit Strategy to Scaffold Novice Program Tracing (SIGCSE)
finding: A 5-10 minute lesson in a memory-table tracing strategy raised tracing scores and cut variance in a small randomized lab study.
numbers: 24 novices, block randomized (13 strategy, 11 control). Tracing total: strategy mean 30.00 (SD 4.91) vs control 24.55 (SD 9.16), p = .049, Cohen's d about 0.72, about 15% higher and 46% less variable. Problem 4 (many variables): p = .021, 11 of 13 perfect. Midterm for 8 strategy respondents: about 7% higher, 42% less variable, p = .083 (not significant).
limits: Very small N; one lab session; the midterm gap was not significant; volunteers.
agent_relevance: A cheap explicit tracing format (a state table) works. Our scaffold can prescribe the table form.

source: Nelson, Xie and Ko (2017) Comprehension First: Evaluating a Novel Pedagogy and Tutoring System for Program Tracing in CS1 (ICER)
finding: A tutor that teaches how programs run by stepping through fixed example programs (a notional machine view) gave larger gains than a writing tutorial (Codecademy) in a small block-randomized study, but the group difference was not statistically significant.
numbers: About 4.33 hours of tutorial; 90 of 200 respondents met inclusion, 41 attended; 18 PLTutor and 19 Codecademy after data loss. SCS1 learning gain 3.89 vs 2.42 of 27 questions (60% higher). Only PLTutor post-test differed from pre-test (p < .0044; Codecademy p < .089). Effect sizes: Cohen's d = .59 (false-to-true, p < .12), .398 (learning gain, p < .41), .34 (percent learned, p < .39). PLTutor gains predicted midterm (R2 = .64); Codecademy adj R2 .18.
limits: Underpowered. Pre-test imbalance (marginal, p about .058-.111). Post-test within about 4.3 hours (carry-over). Self-selected students; single day.
agent_relevance: Tracing-first teaching is promising but not proven. Treat any scaffold gain as a hypothesis to measure ourselves.

source: Nelson, Xie and Ko (2017) Comprehension First: Evaluating a Novel Pedagogy and Tutoring System for Program Tracing in CS1 (ICER)
finding: Framing claim: large multinational studies show most students miss basic execution questions, which motivates tracing-first teaching.
numbers: Text states: more than 60% of students incorrectly answer questions about the execution of basic programs (citing McCracken and Lister groups).
limits: A framing statement; the 60% is from the cited studies, not the new study.
agent_relevance: Baseline human error rate on tracing is high. Compare the agent against it with care.

source: Fincher et al. (2020) Notional Machines in Computing Education: The Education of Attention (ITiCSE WG report)
finding: Systematic review: the notional machine term is widely cited but rarely tested. Hardly any study compares one notional machine to another or tests the idea itself.
numbers: 226 papers extracted. 72% cited NMs only as related work, theory or motivation; 27% identified or used an NM. 116 (just under 50%) defined what they meant by NM. Evaluations: 42 (19%) qualitative, 38 (17%) quantitative, 18 (8%) both. Only 29 papers cited both du Boulay and Sorva 2013.
limits: Search terms may have missed papers (noticeable gap in 2009). The group says no evaluation tested the NM idea itself.
agent_relevance: The central claim that teaching an explicit execution model helps has thin direct causal evidence. Plan to measure it.

source: Fincher et al. (2020) Notional Machines in Computing Education: The Education of Attention (ITiCSE WG report)
finding: Teacher interviews gave 43 example notional machines. There is little research comparing the effectiveness of one against another, or one modality against another. One cited study found non-viable student models and used visualization plus cognitive conflict to repair them.
numbers: Collection of 43 NMs from interviews, papers and software.
limits: Descriptive; no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Several notional machines can coexist (memory table, stack frames, rewriting). The agent should pick one explicitly and keep it fixed per task.

source: Rules of Program Behavior (2021, ACM Transactions on Computing Education)
finding: Proposes writing the notional machine as an explicit ruleset (rules saying how each construct runs) and a progression of rulesets. Theory and design paper with no effect sizes.
numbers: No quantitative result. Notes learners infer their own rules, often too restrictive; cites PLTutor as practice of semantic rules.
limits: Authors acknowledge limited empirical evidence; claims are for design, not outcome.
agent_relevance: A written rules list for the language is a compact notional machine the agent can quote before tracing.

source: Nelson, Xie and Ko (2017) Comprehension First: Evaluating a Novel Pedagogy and Tutoring System for Program Tracing in CS1 (ICER)
finding: Benchmark for scale: end-of-CS1 students score low on the SCS1 tracing-heavy test, so the 3.89-point gain is large next to the course norm.
numbers: Students near the end of a CS1 course score 2 to 20 of 27, mean 9.68, SD 3.5 (SCS1 norm cited by the paper). Within 4.33 hours, 4 PLTutor learners (22%) moved from low scores to over 13.18; one went from 8 to 20.
limits: Anecdotal individual jumps; small groups; pre/post carry-over possible.
agent_relevance: Short, tracing-focused practice can move scores a lot in humans; test whether a trace scaffold does the same for the agent.

source: Lister et al. (2004) multi-national study, question analysis
finding: A tracing question separated strong from weak students sharply: top-quartile students mostly right, bottom quartile near chance.
numbers: Question 2: about 90% of top-quartile students correct vs about 30% of bottom quartile; guessing chance 25% (33% if one option is eliminated).
limits: One question; MCQ with guessable options.
agent_relevance: Use item-level difficulty and guess rate when scoring agent tracing.

source: McCracken et al. (2001) A multi-national, multi-institutional study of assessment of programming skills of first-year CS students
finding: Origin of the claim that most first-year students cannot write working programs; Lister 2004 was designed to test why.
numbers: Recalled, not verified this session: mean score about 22 of 110 points.
limits: Not opened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Sets the human baseline that tracing studies respond to.

source: du Boulay (1986) Some difficulties of learning to program
finding: Introduced the term notional machine: the idealised model of the computer implied by the language's constructs. Learners must build it and many do so wrongly.
numbers: No numbers. The definition is quoted in Fincher 2020 (opened).
limits: Not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Defines what S2 should trace: a named machine model, not real hardware.

source: Sorva (2013) Notional machines and introductory programming education (ACM TOCE 13(2), 8)
finding: Review that made the notional machine a standard term; argues it should be an explicit learning objective.
numbers: No numbers read. Fincher 2020 reports Sorva 2013 is cited as often as du Boulay's original and is the main route into the term.
limits: Not opened; no open PDF found.
agent_relevance: Backs making the machine model explicit in the scaffold.
